In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of epigenetic factors in the natural history of premalignant breast lesions, and with the identification of biological markers that may be used as intermediate endpoints in trials of interventions designed to prevent progression to invasive breast carcinoma.

the development of a model of breast carcinogenesis based on epigenetic factors, and to identify the most appropriate biomarkers for monitoring the effects of intervention on the progression from premalignant breast lesions to invasive cancer.

the role of epigenetic influences in breast cancer and the development of a biological marker strategy to assess the effect in clinical trials of weight reduction, a low-fat diet, or hormone replacement therapy, on the risk of invasive breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the biological markers are useful tools in identifying a subgroup with a higher risk of progression to cancer, but they are not yet sufficiently reliable to be used in clinical practice for this purpose.

there are no biological markers of in situ carcinoma of the type which would allow a prediction of the natural history of individual lesions, but there are some which may allow a prediction of risk of progression to cancer in a population of lesions.
there is no single biological marker that can be used as a reliable predictor of progression to invasive cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk of progression is higher for women whose premalignant lesions show an increase in proliferative activity and/or loss of oestrogen receptor expression, or whose in situ carcinoma is associated with HER-2/neu over-expression.
the risk of progression is increased by obesity and the Western diet, and is reduced by weight loss and the Mediterranean diet.

the biological characteristics of premalignant mammary lesions can be used as surrogate end-points in clinical trials to assess the effect on the risk of breast cancer of weight loss and dietary intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of biomarkers in premalignant breast lesions is influenced by epigenetically induced genetic changes.
the expression of oestradiol receptors in premalignant breast lesions is associated with the presence of the oestrogen receptor in invasive breast cancer.
the expression of oestradiol and progesterone receptors and of HER-2 neu in in situ carcinoma is a good predictor of progression to invasive cancer.
